text: Lesson 6 explores the high adaptability of human beings as shown by numerous human settlements across the world, some even in difficult terrains like hills, deserts, and snowy regions. The students learnt about how humans stay connected for communication and trade through roadways, waterways, railways and technology. In this activity, we will further widen our learning about the human settlements to analyse how the growth of transport and communication in the present day has not provided equal benefits to men and women. text: The Gymnastic Clock M C Davies Main innovative pedagogies are: 1. Warm up activity 2. Poetry escape room 3. Entice them with music 4. Video play 5. PPT for grammar 6. Recitation 7. Use of picture books 8. Worksheets The above activities are come under the following 5’E methods. ENGAGE 1. Warm up activity. Teacher asks the history of clock and collects information about the uses of clock from the students. EXPLORE 1. Poetry escape room A poetry escape room is the most engaging and fun way to introduce or review poetry with your students. The teacher takes some pieces of every 2 lines in the poem and hides behind the walls in a classroom. Students can search and collect

The teacher takes some pieces of every 2 lines in the poem and hides behind the walls in a classroom. Students can search and collect sheet of papers. Finally, they arrange the papers in a sequence order to make a meaningful poetry.

2. Entice them with music Teacher better to begin the gymnastic clock poetry with music which students love it. Music is poetry, it sets a positive atmosphere. Analyzing music as poetry can be powerful and memorable learning experience. EXPLAIN 1. Video play Teacher can show the DSERT’s video of the gymnastic clock poetry which runs under vidyagama programme. Students will come to know the importance of exercises which keeps our body healthy and realizes to build exercises in our daily schedule. 2. PPT for grammar PPT can be shown for glossary, rhyming words and to find the figures of speech which helps to appreciates the poetry. EXPAND 1. Recitation

Poetry recitation and memorizing is a fun activity that you can engage your students to achieve outcomes of the poetry the gymnastic clock 2. Use of picture books Children’s picture books are gold mines for poetry. Prepare a book using some pictures of exercises, clocks, poet’s image, animations along with poetry. Read a book to the entire class or pass out to different small groups and have them to analyze an aspect of the poetry. EVALUATION 1. Worksheets Worksheet 1 How do I know if I am active enough? Instruct students to perform these activities.
Worksheet 3 The puzzle game can help the students about the different types of exercises which keep our body healthy.

Steps for Meditation Practice  Objective of the Meditation Practice To build and strengthen ability to be calm and relax one’s mind and body To re-energize self by connecting to experiences that help to feel safe and secure.  Select a Comfortable Corner Find a comfortable corner in the house; it could also be your balcony, lawn, and terrace full of natural surroundings or a quiet serene corner of one of your rooms where you could spend time with yourself.  Meditation Position  You may choose to sit on a cushion or a mat cross legged (Aasana position) or sit on a chair where you would feel comfortable calm and at ease.  On cushion, mat or chair feel

cross legged (Aasana position) or sit on a chair where you would feel comfortable calm and at ease.  On cushion, mat or chair feel the comfort from the sense of touch to the cushion or the floor.  Sit straight shoulders broad back upright and relaxed.  Head comfortably resting on the spine with chin tucked in slightly.  Keep your face and jaw relaxed.

 Eyes closed or open as you may feel comfortable.  While you prepare for your meditation sitting position, check your body from head to toe for any signs of discomfort. In case of any discomfort, open your eyes and adjust yourself unless you feel comfortable. Please note:-You are requested to not practice in case you are not feeling well in the meditative position or if there is any pain in your body  Breath (5-10 min)  Once you have gained the comfortable posture, take slow deep breath through your nostrils.  Feel the air passing through your lungs to your belly.  Release your breath slowly. Try 3 cycles of breathing in and breathing out.  With each

air passing through your lungs to your belly.  Release your breath slowly. Try 3 cycles of breathing in and breathing out.  With each breath in, feel calm, positive and smile.  With each breath out, feel as if you are releasing all the negativity, anxiety and stress inside.  Start with 3 cycles, and then do 5 and 7 as you get comfortable with the practice.  Calling to Mind a Positive and Joyful Experience (15-20 min)  Once you come to your natural breathing rhythm, try recalling any positive experience that has helped you feel safe, loved and cared for. You could also think about a place, a book or any real or imagined place or situation

helped you feel safe, loved and cared for. You could also think about a place, a book or any real or imagined place or situation that has helped you in difficult times and made you feel safe and comfortable.  Try to recall the details of the experience and notice how you are feeling. What was so beautiful about the experience? What made it such a beautiful experience? Was it the environment? Was it their smile, their care, their conversation, their quiet presence their encouragement or their help.  Stay and Focus on the beauty, kindness of the moment for few minutes.  Try to reflect if the care, the help, the support your received, if that practiced by you
kindness of the moment for few minutes.  Try to reflect if the care, the help, the support your received, if that practiced by you would help you and others.

Closure (5-7 min)  Towards the end, reflect if you developed any skill or insight.  Dedicate any benefit you received out of this practice for the well- being of others in the world.  Focus back on your breath, breathing in calmness, positivity and smile and breathing out worries stress and negativity.  Slowly become aware of the contact with the floor, cushion mat chair.  As you feel comfortable slowly open your eyes and smile. Share or Journal  If you are practicing with a colleague or a friend, if possible share your experience and listen to others experiences.  If practicing alone, keep a Practice Journal log, and write few lines how your experiences was. Students are not able to understand that the sign of the product of negative integers with positive integers depends on the number of negative integers in the product. LET'S CORRECT THIS MISTAKE Students should be given clarity on how ‘-‘ multiplied by ‘-‘ results into a ‘+’ and how this is different from ‘-‘ added with ‘-‘. Properties and operations on integers can be very confusing for students especially when they encounter more than one sign with a number for example: 2 + (-4) x 5 etc. Once they are convinced of this, investigate if they know

more than one sign with a number for example: 2 + (-4) x 5 etc. Once they are convinced of this, investigate if they know the properties of integer operations like commutativity and associativity. Use these to help them extend the rule. The product of 3 negative integers can be considered as a negative integer times the product of two negative integers, that is a negative integer times a positive integer and hence a negative integer. Similarly the product of 4 negative integers (or any even number of negative integers for that matter) can be grouped into products of pairs of negative integers. Each pair will evaluate to a positive integer, and hence the product evaluates to a positive integer.

grouped into products of pairs of negative integers. Each pair will evaluate to a positive integer, and hence the product evaluates to a positive integer. When we do this kind of pairing for a product consisting of an odd number of negative integer, one negative integer remains that cannot be paired off. The product of the negative integers that can be paired off, evaluates to positive. Together with the one that has not been paired, the product becomes negative. You may demonstrate this with a number of examples. Thus help them see that a product consisting of an odd number of negative integers is negative and even number of negative integers is positive. consisting of an odd number of negative integers is negative and even number of negative integers is positive. It is NOT the size of the negative integers that matter, but the number of negative integers in a product. LET'S UNDERSTAND WHERE THE MISTAKE IS HAPPENING... She was given the title īPanditaĬ because she could read and write Sanskrit, a remarkable achievement as women then were not allowed such knowledge. She went on to set up a Mission in Khedgaon near Pune in 1898, where widows and poor women were encouraged not only to become literate but to be independent. They were taught a variety of skills from carpentry to running a printing press, skills that are not usually taught to girls even today. text: SCIENCE 88 When an acidic solution is mixed with a basic solution, both the solutions neutralise the effect of each other. When an acid solution and a base solution are mixed in suitable amounts, both the acidic nature of the acid and the basic nature of the base are destroyed. The resulting solution is neither acidic nor basic. Touch the test tube immediately after neutralisation. What do you observe? In neutralisation reaction, heat is always produced, or evolved. The evolved heat raises the temperature of the reaction mixture. In neutralisation reaction a new substance is formed. This is called salt. Salt may be acidic, basic or neutral in nature. Thus, neutralisation can be defined as follows: The reaction between an
chapter: 7 Class Chapter 4 Acids,Bases and Salts Both Urdu And English Media

text: formed. This is called salt. Salt may be acidic, basic or neutral in nature. Thus, neutralisation can be defined as follows: The reaction between an acid and a base is known as neutralisation. Salt and water are produced in this process with the evolution of heat. Acid+Base  Salt+Water (Heat is evolved) The following reaction is an example: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) + Sodium hydroxide (NaOH)  Sodium chloride (NaCl) + Water (H2O) Boojho added dilute sulphuric acid to lime water. Will the reaction mixture become hot or cool? 4.4 NEUTRALISATION IN EVERYDAY LIFE Indigestion Our stomach contains hydrochloric acid. It helps us to digest food, as you have learnt in Chapter 2. text: stomach contains hydrochloric acid. It helps us to digest food, as you have learnt in Chapter 2. But too much of acid in the stomach causes indigestion. Sometimes indigestion is painful. To relieve indigestion, we take an antacid such as milk of magnesia, which contains magnesium hydroxide. It neutralises the effect of excessive acid. Ant bite When an ant bites, it injects the acidic liquid (formic acid) into the skin. The effect of the acid can be neutralised by rubbing moist baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) or calamine solution, which contains zinc carbonate. Soil treatment Excessive use of chemical fertilisers makes the soil acidic. Plants do not grow well when the soil is either too acidic or too basic. When the

text: use of chemical fertilisers makes the soil acidic. Plants do not grow well when the soil is either too acidic or too basic. When the soil is too acidic, it is treated with bases like quick lime (calcium oxide) or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide). If the soil is basic, organic matter (compost) is added to it. Organic matter releases acids which neutralises the basic nature of the soil. Factory wastes The wastes of many factories contain acids. If they are allowed to flow into the water bodies, the acids will kill fish and other organisms. The factory wastes are, therefore, neutralised by adding basic substances.

text: Measures and relations We can draw squares of different sizes. The perimeter and area change with the length of sides. But in all the squares, the perimeter is always four times the length of side; and the area is the product of the length of side by itself. There are many such situations where even though the measures change, certain relations between them do not change. For example, if we take several objects made of iron, their volume and weight will be different. But if we divide the weight by the volume, we get the same number, 7.8. This is called the density of iron. Similarly if we do this for objects made of copper, weight divided by volume gives
chapter: 7 class digital text book - Kerala State

text: same number, 7.8. This is called the density of iron. Similarly if we do this for objects made of copper, weight divided by volume gives 8.9. This is the density of copper. In such contexts, the unchanging relation between measures is denoted using letters. For example, if we write the weight ofan object made of iron as w and the volume as v, then we can write w= 7.8v If we take copper instead of iron, the relation will be w = 8.9v In general, if the weight of an object is w, its volume is v and if it is made of a material of density d, then their relation can be written as w=dv Measures and numbers One

text: Measures and numbers Numbers were invented by Man to indicate and compare various measurements. For example, instead of saying, “a large group of people”, if we say, “a group of hundred people”, one gets a clear picture. Or instead of saying “walked some distance”, we can be more precise and say, “walked two and a half kilometers”. Length, weight and time are measured directly using instruments; area, volume and density are not directly measured, but are got by computations. For that we need operations with numbers. Learning Resources Data Handling 1. Introduction to Data Handling What is Data? Data refers to a collection of facts, numbers, or information gathered for analysis. For example, the marks of students in a test, daily temperatures, or the number of books in a library are all forms of data. In mathematics, we organize and analyze data to draw meaningful conclusions. Why is Data Handling Important? Data handling helps us: • Summarize large amounts of information. • Make informed decisions (e.g., a teacher analyzing test scores to identify weak areas). • Understand trends and patterns (e.g., average rainfall in a city). Key Terms in Data Handling: • Observation: Each individual value in a dataset (e.g., a student's score). • Range: The

average rainfall in a city). Key Terms in Data Handling: • Observation: Each individual value in a dataset (e.g., a student's score). • Range: The difference between the maximum and minimum values in a dataset. • Arithmetic Mean: The average of all observations. • Mode: The value that appears most frequently. • Median: The middle value when data is arranged in ascending order. 2. Key Concepts 2.1 Range The range measures the spread of data. It is calculated as: Range = Maximum Value - Minimum Value Example: The ages of 5 students are 12, 13, 11, 14, and 10 years. • Maximum = 14, Minimum = 10. • Range = 14 - 10 = 4 years. 2.2 Arithmetic Mean

The arithmetic mean (or average) is the sum of all observations divided by the number of observations. Mean = (Sum of Observations) ÷ (Number of Observations) Example: The marks of 6 students are 70, 85, 60, 90, 75, and 80. • Sum = 70 + 85 + 60 + 90 + 75 + 80 = 460. • Number of observations = 6. • Mean = 460 ÷ 6 ≈ 76.67. 2.3 Mode The mode is the value that appears most often in a dataset. A dataset can have: • One mode (unimodal). • Two modes (bimodal). • No mode (if all values appear equally). Example: The shoe sizes of 7 students are 6, 7, 6, 8, 7, 6, 9. •

(bimodal). • No mode (if all values appear equally). Example: The shoe sizes of 7 students are 6, 7, 6, 8, 7, 6, 9. • 6 appears 3 times, 7 appears 2 times, 8 and 9 appear once. • Mode = 6 (most frequent). 2.4 Median The median is the middle value when data is arranged in ascending order. • For an odd number of observations, it’s the middle term. • For an even number of observations, it’s the average of the two middle terms. Example: The heights (in cm) of 5 students are 150, 145, 160, 155, 148. • Arrange in ascending order: 145, 148, 150, 155, 160. • Middle term (3rd) = 150. • Median = 150 cm.

145, 160, 155, 148. • Arrange in ascending order: 145, 148, 150, 155, 160. • Middle term (3rd) = 150. • Median = 150 cm. Example (Even Number): The weights (in kg) of 6 students are 40, 45, 42, 50, 48, 46. • Arrange in ascending order: 40, 42, 45, 46, 48, 50. • Middle terms = 45 and 46.

Advantages and Limitations • Mean: o Advantage: Represents the entire dataset; useful for averages. o Limitation: Affected by extreme values (e.g., one very high score can skew the mean). • Mode: o Advantage: Shows the most common value; useful for categorical data. o Limitation: May not exist or may not be unique. • Median: o Advantage: Not affected by extreme values; represents the central tendency. o Limitation: Requires data to be ordered, which can be time-consuming for large datasets. Learning Resources Simple Equations 1. Introduction to Simple Equations What is an Equation? An equation is a mathematical statement that shows two expressions are equal, connected by an equals sign (=). For example, (3x + 5 = 11) is an equation where the left side ((3x + 5)) equals the right side (11). Why Study Simple Equations? Equations help us:  Solve unknown quantities in real-life problems (e.g., ﬁnding a person's age or calculating expenses).  Develop logical thinking and problem-solving skills.  Lay the foundation for advanced algebra in higher classes. Key Terms:  Constant: A ﬁxed number (e.g., 5, -7).  Variable: A symbol representing an unknown value (e.g., (x), (y)).  Expression: A combination of constants and

Constant: A ﬁxed number (e.g., 5, -7).  Variable: A symbol representing an unknown value (e.g., (x), (y)).  Expression: A combination of constants and variables (e.g., (2x + 3)).  Equation: Two equal expressions (e.g., (2x + 3 = 7)).  Solution: The value of the variable that makes the equation true (e.g., (x = 2) for (2x = 4)). 2. Key Concepts 2.1 Forming Equations Equations are formed by translating real-life situations or mathematical statements into algebraic expressions.  Example: If a number is increased by 5 and equals 12, the equation is (x + 5 = 12). 2.2 Solving Equations To solve an equation, isolate the variable by performing operations that keep both sides equal. Two common

(x + 5 = 12). 2.2 Solving Equations To solve an equation, isolate the variable by performing operations that keep both sides equal. Two common methods are:  Balancing Method: Perform the same operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division) on both sides.

e Transposition Method: Move terms to the opposite side, changing their sign (e.g., (+5) becomes (-5)). Rules for Solving: e Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the equation balanced. e Multiplying or dividing both sides by the same non-zero number keeps the equation balanced. e Always verify the solution by substituting it back into the original equation. 2.3 Types of Simple Equations e Equations with the variable on one side (e.g., (4x - 3 =9)). e Equations with variables on both sides (e.g., (2x +5 =x + 8)). e Equations involving fractions (e.g., (\frac{x}{3} + 2 = 5)). 2.4 Real-Life Applications Equations are used in: e Budgeting: Calculating expenses or savings. e Age Problems: Determining someone's

fractions (e.g., (\frac{x}{3} + 2 = 5)). 2.4 Real-Life Applications Equations are used in: e Budgeting: Calculating expenses or savings. e Age Problems: Determining someone's age based on relationships. e Distance and Time: Solving problems involving speed or travel. 3. Learning Outcomes By the end of this topic, students will be able to: e Define constants, variables, expressions, and equations. e Form equations from word problems and mathematical statements. e Solve simple linear equations using balancing and transposition methods. e Verify solutions by substituting values. e Apply equations to solve real-life problems. e Appreciate the role of equations in practical scenarios. 4. Detailed Examples Example 1: Solving Using the Balancing Method Problem: Solve (5x - 7 = 18). Solution:

 Step 1: Add 7 to both sides to eliminate (-7): (5x - 7 + 7 = 18 + 7) → (5x = 25).  Step 2: Divide both sides by 5 to isolate (x): (\frac{5x}{5} = \frac{25}{5}) → (x = 5). Veriﬁcation: Substitute (x = 5): (5(5) - 7 = 25 - 7 = 18), which matches the right side. Example 2: Solving Using the Transposition Method Problem: Solve (3y + 4 = 19). Solution:  Step 1: Transpose (+4) to the right, changing it to (-4): (3y = 19 - 4) → (3y = 15).  Step 2: Divide both sides by 3: (y = \frac{15}{3} = 5). Veriﬁcation: Substitute (y = 5): (3(5) + 4 = 15

= 15).  Step 2: Divide both sides by 3: (y = \frac{15}{3} = 5). Veriﬁcation: Substitute (y = 5): (3(5) + 4 = 15 + 4 = 19), which is correct. Example 3: Equation with Variables on Both Sides Problem: Solve (4x + 3 = x + 12). Solution:  Step 1: Subtract (x) from both sides to get variables on one side: (4x - x + 3 = 12) → (3x + 3 = 12).  Step 2: Subtract 3 from both sides: (3x = 12 - 3 = 9).  Step 3: Divide by 3: (x = \frac{9}{3} = 3). Veriﬁcation: Substitute (x = 3): Left side: (4(3) + 3 = 12 + 3 = 15). Right

Divide by 3: (x = \frac{9}{3} = 3). Veriﬁcation: Substitute (x = 3): Left side: (4(3) + 3 = 12 + 3 = 15). Right side: (3 + 12 = 15). Both sides are equal. Example 4: Real-Life Word Problem Problem: The cost of 3 notebooks is ₹45. Find the cost of one notebook. Solution:  Let the cost of one notebook be (x) rupees.

 Equation: (3x = 45).  Divide both sides by 3: (x = \frac{45}{3} = 15).  Cost of one notebook = ₹15. Veriﬁcation: (3 \times 15 = 45), which matches the given cost. 5. Learning Resources The Triangles and its properties 1. Introduction to Triangles What is a Triangle? A triangle is a closed ﬁgure formed by three line segments, with three vertices, three sides, and three angles. It is the simplest polygon and a fundamental shape in geometry. Why Study Triangles?  Triangles are the building blocks of many geometric shapes and structures.  Their properties are used in construction, design, and engineering.  Understanding triangles lays the foundation for advanced geometry topics like trigonometry. Key Terms:  Vertex: A point where two sides meet (e.g., A, B, C in △ABC).  Side: A line segment connecting two vertices (e.g., AB, BC, CA).  Angle: The measure between two sides at a vertex

Key Concepts 2.1 Types of Triangles  Based on Sides: o Equilateral: All sides equal; all angles equal (60° each). o Isosceles: Two sides equal; two angles opposite those sides equal. o Scalene: All sides and angles unequal.  Based on Angles: o Acute-angled: All angles less than 90°. o Right-angled: One angle equals 90°. o Obtuse-angled: One angle greater than

text: 2.2 Properties of Triangles Angle Sum Property: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°. Exterior Angle Property: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Triangle Inequality: The sum of any two sides is greater than the third side. Pythagoras Property: In a right-angled triangle, (a*2 + b*2 = c*2), where (c) is the hypotenuse (side opposite the right angle). 2.3 Medians and Altitudes Median: Divides the opposite side into two equal parts. A triangle has three medians, meeting at the centroid. Altitude: Perpendicular to the opposite side. A triangle has three altitudes, meeting at the orthocenter. Difference: A median connects to the midpoint; an altitude is perpendicular but may not be

Difference: A median connects to the midpoint; an altitude is perpendicular but may not be at the midpoint. 2.4 Real-Life Applications Triangles are used in: Construction: Ensuring stable structures like bridges and roofs. Surveying: Measuring land areas using triangulation. Design: Creating aesthetic patterns in art and architecture. Navigation: Calculating distances using triangular paths. 3. The NCF-2005 also lays emphasis on development in the children logical abilities as well as abilities to comprehend space, spatial transformations and develop the ability to visualise both these. It recommends that mathematics needs to slowly move towards abstraction even though it starts from concrete experiences and models. The ability to generalise and perceive patterns is an important step in being able to relate

even though it starts from concrete experiences and models. We also know that most children in upper primary and secondary classes develop a fear of mathematics and it is one of the reasons for students not being able to continue in schools. A Note for the Teachers This book is a continuation of the process and builds on what was initiated in Class VI. We had shared with you the main points reflected in NCF-2005. These include relating mathematics to a wider development of abilities in children, moving away from complex calculations and algorithms following, to understanding and constructing a framework of understanding. The mathematical ideas in the mind of the child grow neither by telling nor by merely giving explanations. For children to learn mathematics, to be confident in it and understand the foundational ideas, they need to develop their own framework of concepts. This would require a classroom where children discuss ideas, look for solutions of problems, set new problems

need to develop their own framework of concepts. This would require a classroom where children discuss ideas, look for solutions of problems, set new problems and find not only their own ways of solving problems but also their own definitions with the language they can use and understand. These definitions need not be as general and complete as the standard ones. In the mathematics class it is important to help children read with understanding the textbook and other references. The reading of materials is not normally considered to be related to learning of mathematics but learning mathematics any further would require the child to comprehend the text. The text in mathematics uses a language that has brevity. It requires the

learning mathematics any further would require the child to comprehend the text. The text in mathematics uses a language that has brevity. It requires the ability to deal with terseness and with symbols, to follow logical arguments and appreciate the need for keeping certain factors and constraints. Children need practice in translating mathematical statements into normal statements expressing ideas in words and vice-a-versa. We would require children to become confident of using language in words and also being able to communicate through mathematical statements. Mathematics at the upper primary stage is a major challenge and has to perform the dual role of being both close to the experience and environment of the child and being abstract. Children often are not

has to perform the dual role of being both close to the experience and environment of the child and being abstract. Children often are not able to work in terms of ideas alone. They need the comfort of context and/or models linked to their experience to find meaning. This stage presents before us the challenge of engaging the children while using the contexts but gradually moving them away from such dependence. So while children should be able to identify the principles to be used in a contextual situation, they should not be dependent or be limited to contexts. Learning mathematics is not about remembering solutions or methods but knowing how to solve problems. Problem-solving strategies give learners opportunities to think rationally, enabling them to understand and create methods as well as processes; they become active participants in the construction of new knowledge rather than being passive receivers. Learners need to identify and define a problem, select or design possible solutions and revise or redesign the steps, if required. On being presented a problem, children first need to decode it. They need to identify the knowledge required for attempting it and build a model for it. This model could be in the form of an illustration or a situation construct. We must remember that for generating proofs in geometry the figures constructed are also models of the ideal dimensionless figure. These diagrams are, however, more abstract than the concrete models required for attempting problems in arithmetic and algebra. This should replace prescriptive algorithms to solve problems. Teachers are expected to encourage cooperative learning. Children learn a lot in purposeful conversation with each other. Our classrooms should develop in the students the desire and capacity to learn from each other rather than compete. Conversation is not noise and consultation is not cheating. It is a challenge to make possible classroom groups that benefit the most from being with each other

Archimedes, a Greek scientist, is said to have done just that more than two thousand years ago. When the Romans attacked Syracuse, a coastal city-state in Greece, Archimedes used mirrors arranged as shown in Fig. 11.34. The mirrors could be moved in any direction. text: 7.8 From the Rulers to The Ruled Types of Government Learning Resource: From the Rulers to the Ruled – Types of Government What is Government? A government is the system by which a country or community is ruled. • It makes laws. • It protects citizens. • It manages resources and ensures order. Types of Government • Monarchy o Rule by a king or queen. o Power is inherited (passed from parent to child). o Example: Ancient kingdoms of India, modern Britain (constitutional monarchy). • Dictatorship o Rule by one person with complete power. o Citizens have little or no freedom. o Example: Some 20th-century regimes. • Democracy o Rule by the people, through elected representatives. o Citizens have rights
chapter: 7 SEM1-EM-L8 "From the Rulers to The Ruled Types of Government"

text: Citizens have little or no freedom. o Example: Some 20th-century regimes. • Democracy o Rule by the people, through elected representatives. o Citizens have rights and freedoms. o Example: India today. • Republic o Head of state is elected, not a king. o India is a democratic republic. From Rulers to the Ruled • In ancient times, rulers (kings, emperors) had absolute power. • Over time, people demanded rights and participation. • Today, most countries have democratic governments where citizens elect leaders. Key Concepts • Government ensures law and order. • Different systems give different levels of freedom to citizens. • India shifted from rule by kings/emperors to a democratic republic after independence. text: 7.9 From the Barter to Money 1. Barter System – The Beginning 1. Meaning: Exchange of goods for goods without using money. E.g., farmer gives wheat to potter for pots. 2. Problems of barter: - Double coincidence of wants: Both people must want what the other has. - No common measure: Difficult to decide how much wheat = 1 pot. - No storage of value: Can’t store grains for long, they get spoilt. - Not divisible: Can’t divide a cow to buy small items. 2. Invention of Money 1. Why money: To solve problems of barter. Money became a medium of exchange. 2. Early forms: Grains, cattle, shells, stones, metal pieces used as money. 3. 7.10 UNDERSTARTING MARKETS What is a Market? A market is not just a place — it is a system where buyers and sellers interact. • It can be a physical space (weekly bazaar, shops, malls). • It can also be virtual (online shopping platforms). • The key idea: A market exists wherever goods and services are exchanged. Types of Markets • Weekly Market o Held once or twice a week. o Goods are cheaper because they come directly from producers. o Example: Vegetable markets in towns. • Shops o Permanent, open daily. o Sell branded and non-branded goods. o Example: Stationery shops, grocery stores. • Shopping Complex/Malls o Large buildings with many shops under one roof. o Goods are usually

and non-branded goods. o Example: Stationery shops, grocery stores. • Shopping Complex/Malls o Large buildings with many shops under one roof. o Goods are usually branded, prices are higher. • Online Market o Websites/apps like Amazon, Flipkart. o Goods delivered to your doorstep. Participants in the Market • Producers: Make goods (farmers, factory owners). • Traders: Middlemen who buy from producers and sell to shops. • Shopkeepers: Sell directly to consumers. • Consumers: People who buy goods for use. 7.9 FROM BARTER TO MONEY The Evolution of Trade 🪙 Before coins and banknotes existed, people used different systems to get what they needed. This journey is usually divided into a few key milestones: 1. The Barter System: The direct exchange of goods and services without using money. For example, swapping a bag of wheat for a pair of shoes . 2. Commodity Money: Using items with intrinsic value (like salt, shells, or grain) as a medium of exchange. 3. Metallic Money: The introduction of coins made from precious metals like gold and silver . 4. Paper Money and Modern Banking: The shift to banknotes and, eventually, digital transactions like credit cards and UPI. Understanding the Barter System The Barter

4. Paper Money and Modern Banking: The shift to banknotes and, eventually, digital transactions like credit cards and UPI. Understanding the Barter System The Barter System is the oldest form of trade. However, for it to work, a very specific condition must be met called the "Double Coincidence of Wants." This means that both parties must simultaneously have what the other person wants. If I have apples and want bread, I have to find someone who has bread and specifically wants apples. If they want milk instead, the trade can't happen! To get us started, can you think of a reason why the Barter System might be difficult to use if you were trying to trade something big, like a

can you think of a reason why the Barter System might be difficult to use if you were trying to trade something big, like a cow , for something small, like a loaf of bread ? The jump from trading goods to using money happened because bartering had some big "pain points." Besides the Double Coincidence of Wants, traders faced problems like: • Store of Value: How do you save your wealth if your "money" is perishable, like fish or vegetables ? • Measure of Value: How do you decide exactly how many eggs are equal to one goat ? • Divisibility: If you want to buy something small but only have a large animal to trade, you can't exactly

equal to one goat ? • Divisibility: If you want to buy something small but only have a large animal to trade, you can't exactly "split" the animal without losing its value! To solve these, people started using Commodity Money—items that everyone in a community agreed were valuable, such as salt , cattle , or even beautiful cowrie shells . Eventually, these were replaced by Metallic Money (coins), which were easier to carry, didn't spoil, and could be stamped with a seal to prove their weight and purity. Janapadas and Mahājanapadas Towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, regional cultures gradually reorganised themselves in north India. As people formed clans or groups, probably sharing a common language and common customs, each clan came to be associated with a territory or janapada led by a rājā or ruler. (‘Janapada’ is a Sanskrit word which means ‘where the people (jana) have set foot (pada),’ that is, have settled down.) The janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them. most of the water comes down through the branches or leaves of the trees. The roots of the trees help the water to seep down in the ground. Explain: Viewing objects by slicing One way to view a 3D object is by cutting or slicing it to obtain its cross-section. A cross-section is the exposed surface of a solid that you get when you cut through it. Thus, it does not contain any piece of the original face. It all comes from “inside” the object. Let us take an example of a cheese block: The cheese block is like a cuboid with a

It all comes from “inside” the object. Let us take an example of a cheese block: The cheese block is like a cuboid with a square face. A square cross-section is obtained if you slice or cut it vertically with a knife. And when you slice it horizontally, a rectangular cross-section is obtained. Similarly, you can slice along different axes to get different cross-sections of solids. (Teacher can use any empty box, notebook, pencil box, or other 3D objects). Period 2.8: Feeding and Digestion in amoeba Concepts Covered: FEEDING AND DIGESTION IN AMOEBA Amoeba is a single-celled organism commonly found in water bodies such as ponds and lakes. It has a simple yet fascinating way of capturing and digesting food. Using pseudopodia, or finger-like projections of its cell membrane, it engulfs food particles through a process called phagocytosis. Once engulfed, the food is digested inside a food vacuole with the help of enzymes, and nutrients are absorbed into the cytoplasm. Grammar (Reported Speech) Teaching Learning Process Hook: The teacher selects 3-4 students to say a short and simple sentence, which is then written on the board with quotation marks. After each sentence, the teacher immediately repeats what the student said and writes it on the board without using quotation marks. For example: The student says: “I like chocolate!” The teacher repeats: "He/She said that he/she liked chocolate."

Experience and reflection Think and write about two instances when someone shared something important or interesting with you. Example: My mom said that helping others makes you feel happy. Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) The teacher explains direct speech and reported speech with examples by writing them on the board. Direct Speech is used to repeat the exact words spoken by someone, and we use quotation marks (" ") to show this in writing. Example: “I like chocolate!” Reported Speech is used when you want to tell someone what someone

quotation marks (" ") to show this in writing. Example: “I like chocolate!” Reported Speech is used when you want to tell someone what someone else has said, but without using the exact words (no quotation marks). Example: He said that he liked chocolate. Demonstrating with an example: Direct Speech: “How much did you pay for that hilsa?” the woman asked. Reported Speech: The woman asked the man how much he had paid for that hilsa. What changes do you observe in the pronoun, tense, and sentence structure? (Take student responses) ● Tense Change: The verb "did" in the direct speech is changed to "had" in the reported speech (present tense to past perfect tense). Example: "Did you pay" →
verb "did" in the direct speech is changed to "had" in the reported speech (present tense to past perfect tense). Example: "Did you pay" → "he had paid." ● Question Mark Becomes a Statement:

100 The question mark in the direct speech is replaced by a full stop, turning the question into a statement. Example: "How much did you pay?" → "The woman asked how much he had paid." ● Pronouns Change: The pronoun "you" in the direct speech changes to "he" in the reported speech. Example: "you" → "he." We change the sentence structure, usually without quotation marks, and sometimes adjust the pronoun and tense. CFU (Open-ended/ Factual) Factual 1. Tally marks are a simple technique for recording the number of objects and keeping track of counting in groups of five. Using tally marks, vertical lines like “|” represent the first four counts. The old man and his wife had no children, so they treated Muko like their own child. They fed him from their own plates, and the dog loved them dearly. Every morning, Muko followed the old man to the fields. One day, Muko led his master to a certain spot and started scratching the ground. When the old man dug there, he found a pile of gold coins! Chivvy (Poem) Poet: Michael Rosen Summary: The poem “Chivvy” by Michael Rosen is a humorous and thoughtful poem that talks about how adults constantly nag children by giving too many instructions. It starts with a list of things that children are told repeatedly, such as: Speak up Don’t talk with your mouth full Say please Don’t interrupt Pull your socks up

of things that children are told repeatedly, such as: Speak up Don’t talk with your mouth full Say please Don’t interrupt Pull your socks up Sit straight Take your hands out of your pockets Say thank you Don’t drag your feet The poet shows that this continuous ‘chivvying’ (nagging) makes children feel frustrated and helpless. The same adults who constantly control them later ask them to “make their own decisions”, which sounds unfair and confusing. The poem highlights the problem of too much control over children and the lack of freedom they face. It is funny, sarcastic, and critical of adult behaviour. Rusting of Iron Rusting is a slow chemical change that occurs when iron reacts with oxygen and water, forming iron oxide (rust). This process is destructive and weakens iron structures. Rusting can be prevented by: ● Painting or greasing to block air and moisture. ● Galvanization, where a layer of zinc is coated on iron to prevent direct contact with air and water. Crystallization Crystallization is a process used to obtain pure substances from solutions. It is an example of a physical change. Large, well-formed crystals can be obtained through slow cooling of saturated solutions (e.g., purification of salts

solutions. It is an example of a physical change. Large, well-formed crystals can be obtained through slow cooling of saturated solutions (e.g., purification of salts like copper sulfate). Chemical Reactions and Bonding A chemical reaction is a process where one or more substances (reactants) undergo a transformation to form new substances (products). Chemical bonding plays a crucial role in these reactions. Some examples of chemical reactions include: ● Burning of magnesium ribbon (formation of magnesium oxide). ● Reaction of copper sulfate solution with iron (formation of iron sulfate and copper). ● Vinegar and baking soda reaction (carbon dioxide gas formation). Circulatory system in Animals: ● The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, and waste products within the body. ● Blood consists of plasma, red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets. ● RBCs contain haemoglobin, which helps transport oxygen. ● WBCs play a role in fighting infections and protecting the body. ● Platelets help in blood clotting to prevent excessive bleeding. ● Blood vessels include: ○ Arteries – Carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the body. ○ Veins – Carry carbon dioxide-rich blood back to the heart. ○ Capillaries – Facilitate the exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste. ● The heart is a four-chambered organ that pumps blood continuously. ● Heartbeats are the rhythmic contractions and relaxations of

of oxygen, nutrients, and waste. ● The heart is a four-chambered organ that pumps blood continuously. ● Heartbeats are the rhythmic contractions and relaxations of the heart muscles. ● A stethoscope is used to measure heartbeats. ● Pulse rate indicates heart activity and varies with physical exertion. Excretion in Animals: ● The process of removing waste products from the body. ● The human excretory system includes kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra. ● Kidneys filter waste from the blood, forming urine. ● Other excretory processes include sweating (removes salts and water) and exhalation (removes carbon dioxide). ● Different animals excrete waste in different forms (e.g., fish release ammonia, birds excrete uric acid). Transportation in Plants: ● Root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil. ● Xylem transports water and minerals from roots to leaves. ● Phloem transports food (glucose) from leaves to other parts of the plant. ● Transpiration (loss of water through leaves) helps pull water upward and cools the plant. ● Stomata are tiny openings on leaves that control water loss and gas exchange.
